TMT Credit Research  
ORCL Credit: Higher Rates, Higher Stakes  
| | [Read Full Report](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/5afe5886-c8bb-11f1-a2f0-77fc022c1a94?t=1792118648:1668:9323:5e2e4f67363b&m=1&ch=CDF Research ISG#e=ZmVsaXBlLm1vbnRlaXJvQGNhcHN0b25lLmNvbS5icg==)  
---  
(PDF: 7 Pages)  
---  
| North America  
---  
Lindsay A Tyler, David M Hamburger  
October 16, 2026  
---  
The higher rate environment has driven meaningful spread widening across high-
beta lower-quality IG TMT credits, notably ORCL, CHTR and SKYD, with similar
parallel moves WoW up until Thursday's session. Despite a higher rating, ORCL
appears particularly exposed given its capital-intensive GPUaaS model and
dependence on sizable debt financing to fund upfront buildout costs. As of
Thursday's close, ORCL's implied 10Y YTW has risen ~150bp since the start of
CY2H, with cash and CDS spreads widening >25bp WoW and >50bp MoM.Further,
these moves – alongside volatility in the CRWV complex – underscore how the
higher-rate environment is amplifying credit differentiation between high-
quality IG issuers and lower-quality AI players, including ORCL, CRWV and
shell project finance. Higher funding costs can create a negative flywheel
between buildout economics, market access, execution and investor sentiment.We
are finding investor scrutiny is increasingly converging on risks long central
to our ORCL thesis: funding needs, off-balance-sheet exposure, contract
durability, counterparty quality, shell lease/customer contract mismatches,
ecosystem circularity, possible delivery delays (discussed
[here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/ebd72d32-b82c-11f1-a440-99a719172027?ch=rp&sch=ar))
and a possibly crowded chip financing market (discussed
[here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/14b70596-c300-11f1-9a76-0c9193771472?ch=rp&sch=ar)).Implications
of Higher Funding Costs

  1.  _Possible shift in funding approach to finance the existing buildout._ ORCL remains early in its data center buildout, with substantial funding needs ahead (illustrated [here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/7a702140-ad63-11f1-8ecd-723b2bfc0461?ch=rp&sch=ar#/exhibit=1)) and limited flexibility around contracts and leases. We expect greater reliance on ~5Y asset-backed chip financing, an avenue we've long highlighted and now the subject of recent unconfirmed press (discussed [here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/14b70596-c300-11f1-9a76-0c9193771472?ch=rp&sch=ar)). While feasible, such paper may face competition from other deals, and pricing will probably still exceed traditional BBB levels. Higher funding costs may also constrain currency diversification, increase reliance on costly equity, and alter the role of customer prepayments.
  2. _Potential ratings pressure._ We have long expected a Moody's downgrade to Baa3 based on our gross adjusted leverage forecasts relative to the agency's threshold (as illustrated [here](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/7a702140-ad63-11f1-8ecd-723b2bfc0461?ch=rp&sch=ar#/exhibit=3)). Sharply higher funding costs could accelerate that outcome given the needs ahead, but precedent is limited. 
  3. _Rethinking further expansion._ While ORCL has framed its buildout at ~10GW, management's enthusiasm for customer prepayments and an estimated ~1GW of lease pre-signings this quarter suggest appetite for further expansion, particularly given higher revenue-per-watt economics elsewhere. But developers and powered-shell-providers may increasingly prefer HQ IG counterparties given widening funding-cost differentials and growing concentration concerns. The implications of the constraints are mixed: the benefit of avoiding additional capex offset by foregone growth.

Maintaining a Cautious Stance Ahead of Analyst DayWhile Thursday's intraday
recovery – aided by NVDA management commentary and the crossing of notable
spread levels (~300/250/300bp in 5Y CDS/10Y/30Y) – is encouraging, we remain
cautious on risk/reward and would be hesitant to step in ahead of the October
28 Analyst Day in Las Vegas.In hindsight, our earlier fundamental view and
initial spread targets (~200/200/250bp in 5Y CDS/35s/55s) may have considered
ORCL too much in isolation. Broader market forces have since compounded the
pressure, prompting us to remove specific targets a couple of months ago while
maintaining our trades. AI-related supply began weighing even on higher-
quality issuers over the summer, while ORCL now contends with higher rates,
high-beta IG TMT volatility and elevated bespoke chip-financing supply.Looking
ahead, even largely unchanged Analyst Day messaging could initially be well
received, given the historically low bar for communication and investors'
tendency to initially favor bullish interpretations of ORCL developments.
Ultimately, however, we suspect the heightened volatility and scrutiny may
matter more than the messaging as investors await tangible progress. Plus, a
wider peer comp set complicates the historical bull case that ORCL's wide
spreads and commitment to IG sufficiently compensate for the risks.We continue
to expect CDS to underperform cash bonds should bondholder hedging emerge,
particularly if hypothetical chip-lease financing participants also seek
protection. That said, we maintain our select sell cash bond recommendations,
while flagging potential 10Y underperformance vs. 30Y. Specifically, we see
potential for modest spread-curve flattening, in 5s30s and potentially 10s30s,
reflecting the possible shorter-dated financing approach, possible distressed
demand for longer bonds at low dollar prices and yields north of 8%, and
potential liability-management risk (in sub-$65).NVDA and the Question of
SupportAs funding tightens for select names, markets may increasingly look to
stronger balance sheets, including semiconductor vendors, to facilitate
financing or absorb risk. We remain neutral on NVDA credit but see potential
for CDS underperformance versus cash from support-related hedging.As discussed
in our
[initiation](https://ny.matrix.ms.com/eqr/article/webapp/29875000-9ce2-11f1-b5c5-f551449e1153?ch=rp&sch=ar),
NVDA has outlined various forms of chip/compute support, including unused-
capacity arrangements, price floors (more relevant for neoclouds pursuing
shorter, higher-revenue-per-watt contracts), and residual-value support (more
relevant for players without contracted demand). Key questions remain around
beneficiaries, terms and structures. It does not appear NVDA plans to
prioritize IG counterparties beyond chip allocation, and any hypothetical deal
involving GPUs does not necessarily imply explicit NVDA support.Explicit
support for ORCL from NVDA or another well-capitalized partner remains the
most meaningful positive catalyst we envision and a key risk to our cautious
view. However, NVDA's growing contingent commitments – and probable heightened
scrutiny of such arrangements with this backdrop – make the credit value of
additional support less clear-cut than before.Other Recent Related Content:

By [Erica R Spear

[Click here for the full document and
disclaimers](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14215810&ad=5013176812&h=eZjC3dT&sig=NsPFFa6QtaP7yWZG6Ih5rXAsPXc&v=2&isig=ZkXK1HFLGdjRFWzgDllgnotTMsz&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/t586441i/GPS-5484229-0/69310712-e0a4-41cd-a14f-9e0acde5ed14)

In today’s TMT weekly, we first discuss CRWV weakness and AI financing
concerns before turning to news out of ACN and AMAT’s investor days, updates
on ORCL’s Project Jupiter, and more.

  * Theme of the Week — Will the Circle Be Unbroken?: Recent weakness in CoreWeave, alongside higher Treasury yields, has renewed scrutiny of financing costs and risks associated with AI infrastructure investment this week. While we do not view financial distress at CRWV as our base case, a more severe liquidity event or restructuring could disrupt contracted computing capacity, expose lenders to losses and raise questions around GPU collateral values and financing structures. We see particular implications for NVIDIA, given its role as CRWV’s primary GPU supplier, equity investor and contracted capacity purchaser, although its substantial financial capacity and strategic incentives could support efforts to mitigate disruption. On that note, NVDA CEO Jensen Huang said yesterday that “CoreWeave’s strength is improving everyday,” and “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.” The reiterated support led CRWV shares to close up 6% yesterday (vs. SPX +0.3%) after selling off meaningfully earlier in the week. A negative outcome at CRWV would raise serious questions about the viability of the AI trade and also weigh on hyperscaler spreads, primarily through sentiment and sector technicals, though names like MSFT, META and GOOGL have billions in leases tied to CRWV. Meanwhile, higher Treasury yields could further complicate AI financing, particularly for data center and GPU project finance structures where borrowing costs and residual value assumptions are critical to transaction economics. We expect most hyperscalers' investment plans to remain relatively insensitive to rates given strong cash generation and strategic priorities, with ORCL a notable exception due to its greater reliance on external financing. That said, higher financing costs and tighter lending standards could reduce leverage capacity, delay execution or challenge the economics of planned financing packages, particularly those involving weaker counterparties or greater residual value exposure. Nevertheless, we continue to expect substantial AI investment, with financing challenges more likely to affect individual infrastructure providers than the broader hyperscaler investment cycle at this point.
  * Trade of the Week: in [Spotlight](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14215810&ad=5013176812&h=c_tgdJX&sig=DQvq1v7iUuv0ezmoaS16gvzjd7a&v=2&isig=YQU1ty0mSqTGG3qx7BFOfkh9Mp3&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/email/scx/-hq1mup7/GPS-5488921-0/69310712-e0a4-41cd-a14f-9e0acde5ed14) this week we recommended a short on META 6.30% ‘56s ahead of results and potential supply next week.
  * Primary Markets YTD TMT supply remained unchanged at $446bn with most issuers now in earnings blackout.
  * Secondary markets were 2.5bps wider, though all TMT subsectors materially underperformed on the back of AI financing concerns, a hot CPI print and volatile rates.
  * Next week, 3Q earnings begin in full force and we look forward to hearing from META, CMCSA, IBM, T, NFLX and several others.

# CoreWeave

## Debt Concerns Reflect Sentiment Around Timing of Cash Flows, Contrary to
Healthy Contract Economics, Returns and Execution Leadership in Scaling

  
---  
  
By [Samik Chatterjee, CFA
AC](https://jpmorgan.email.streetcontxt.net/platform/al?a=14215240&ad=5012557239&h=kgwv39I&sig=CBQS46j0J0Uw6heNIzryMlAq04s&v=2&url=https://markets.jpmorgan.com/research/analyst/J966524),

CRWV, CRWV US  
Price (15 Oct 26):$69.69  
  
CoreWeave shares have declined ~20% this week, with the repricing led by
concerns around increase in bond yields and compounded likely by Gartner's
forecast published this week which expressed concerns around AI revenue
required to support healthy returns for NeoClouds, which together are driving
investor concerns around overcapacity and the sustainability of debt funding.
While we understand that the valuation multiple on CRWV shares is dictated not
only by CoreWeave's own fundamentals but also by investor appetite for its
datacenter debt more broadly, we believe the current concerns are overdone
relative to the fundamentals of the business, on account of: 1) Datacenter
demand is robust and has improved in recent months, rather than moderated,
providing limited datapoints to support long-term datacenter demand concerns;
2) Bringing capacity online is materially tougher than the linear progression
in relation to conversion of published contracted capacity to active capacity,
and CoreWeave's execution leadership on this front has consistently stood out
in our customer conversations; 3) Economics at a project level remain sound
with the company positioned to generate both healthy margins and returns on
cash flow, despite initial investment focus driving some temporary margin and
cash flow hurdles; 4) Beyond the sound economics on a project for a typical
5-year contract agreement, there is an additional monetization lever in
recontracting GPUs beyond the 5-year duration; and 5) Project level returns
(unlevered IRR) exceed cost of capital for the company, and increases in cost
of capital are likely to be embedded into pricing of new projects. While we
acknowledge the increase in cost of capital in relation to the recent concerns
in the debt market and the rising yields can potentially limit the headroom to
generate positive returns, we believe the favorable demand backdrop for
compute enables pricing power to pass the cost through to customers and limit
change to the fundamentals of the revenue/ profit model.

  * Capacity is pre-sold under long-term take-or-pay contracts rather than building for estimated demand. Gartner's forecast on an industry-level gap between the $8.5T of cumulative revenue it estimates AI data center owners need through 2030 to earn a 12% return on invested capital and the no more than $3.6T of AI revenue it forecasts over the same period, implies risk for capacity brought online ahead of demand rather than for CoreWeave which brings capacity online that has been pre-sold under long-term contracts to customers. Additionally, relative to concerns expressed by Gartner, recent months have showcased an acceleration of compute demand, rather than a deceleration, providing limited datapoints to support concerns around long-term demand. However, in the scenario that investors are concerned about demand durability and ability to lease uncontracted capacity, with more than 2/3rds of a typical datacenter capex attributable to technology and short-lived assets relative to a datacenter shell, the time horizon to throttle capex is short and limits risks around long-term cash outflows.
  * Overcapacity is less of a concern as active capacity conversion from planned capacity needs strong execution, which puts CoreWeave in a leading position. As much as it seems simple to linearly project industry capacity from announced plans, bringing capacity online is materially tougher than contracting it, and in our customer conversations CoreWeave remains in a leading position in relation to executing to plans and delivering to timelines. CoreWeave added nearly 500MW in F2Q26 alone to reach 1.5GW of active power, with contracted power at 4.2GW as of Aug 11 relative to the target of at least 8GW by 2030.
  * Contract economics generate residual cash flow to the parent, with GPU useful lives extending the optionality beyond the contract term. As laid out in the company's illustrative contract cash flow (Figure 1), a 5-year contract with capex of ~51% of total contract value, funded ~80% by asset-level debt, generates residual cash flow to the parent of ~16% of contract value after full repayment of the asset-level debt, sufficient to cover ~5 years of data center obligations even if the capacity is not re-contracted. We view the illustrative economics as conservative, as the useful lives of GPUs are currently extending beyond both the 6-year depreciation schedule and the contract term, as evidenced by observed in-market usage of ~8 years on V100 and ~7 years on T4 and the A100 contract signed into 2029 on a SKU introduced in 2020, positioning CoreWeave to earn cash flow beyond the contract term with only lease and power costs to cover once the asset-level debt is repaid.

Figure 1: Contract Economics

![](cid:67470860-a071-4a60-ba76-990360c96593@jpmorgan.com)

Source: Company presentation

  * Project returns clear the blended cost of capital. As outlined below in the illustrative IRR calculation, we estimate unlevered contract IRR in the mid-teens range, relative to a blended cost of capital in the range of 9%-11% assuming the vast majority of the capex will be funded by a combination of parent company and asset backed debt, for a typical 5-year contract duration. However, with the likelihood of a contract renewal beyond the initial 5-year duration, the IRR rises to a higher level relative to the mid-teens. Additionally, while we acknowledge the likelihood of an increase in cost of capital with the current concerns in the debt market, we expect the pricing for compute for new capacity to embed the higher cost to keep return fundamentals unchanged for the company. 

Figure 2: Illustrative Project-Level IRR Calculation

![](cid:aaead88f-881b-45b1-8a7f-499c3df5814d@jpmorgan.com)

Source: J.P. Morgan, Company presentations

  * Near-term funding needs are high, but more on account of a steep capacity ramp; need scale to generate free cash flow while adding capacity rapidly. The planned ramp of active capacity from 1.85 GW exiting this year to 8GW in 2030, implies 4x increase in 4 years or adding about 1.5GW each year relative to the current 500MW added in 2025 and 1GW expected to be added in 2026. With simplistic economics of revenue of $10-$15B per GW annually once a project is fully ramped and $35B+ of capex per GW in the ramp year for a project, the company needs the installed base of stabilized projects to be 4-5x the capacity being ramped in a year to start generating cash after covering for the capex directed towards new capacity. The above economics, also shown in Figure 4 below, outlines that the cash burn is not a function of unfavorable economics per project but more on account of the capacity being ramped each year relative to the installed active capacity at this time.

Figure 3: Illustrative Per-GW Economics

![](cid:f6a15edd-2704-40d7-901d-ace1eeac5c82@jpmorgan.com)

Note: Revenue at midpoint of $10-15B/GW, cash EBITDA at ~75% contract level
margin

Source: J.P. Morgan, Company reports

As shown in the figure below, active power at the start of the year relative
to the power added in the year is currently running at roughly 1:1, with
CoreWeave entering 2026 with ~0.85GW of active power against ~1GW expected to
be added through the year, and the ratio remaining close to that level at
~1.2x in 2027E as the company adds ~1.5GW annually on the path to its 8GW
target. In our view, this ratio needs to be ~4-5x for the cash EBITDA
generated by the installed base, at a ~75% EBITDA margin on $10-15B of annual
revenue per GW, to cover the ~$35B of capex per GW directed towards new
capacity, which on our illustrative ramp is reached only in 2030E at ~4.5x. As
such, we view the current cash burn as a function of the pace of the capacity
ramp relative to the installed base, with the timing of FCF generation largely
remediated as CoreWeave scales.

## Cloud, Software & Internet

**MSFT (Neutral) - Completes pre-training of 2.8tn-parameter MAI-Base-2,
claiming 4-12x efficiency over the best open base model**  
Microsoft AI (led by Mustafa Suleyman) has finished pre-training MAI-Base-2, a
mixture-of-experts foundation model with 2.8tn total and 80bn active
parameters and native text-image input, trained over 38 days in August-
September on 16,000 Nvidia GB200 GPUs using a 50tn-token dataset (21% average
MFU, 89% goodput). Microsoft says it beats every open-weight model it tested
on held-out evaluations and is 4.2-12.3x more pre-training-FLOPs-efficient
than DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base, the strongest open base model, and 6.3-12.7x more
efficient than its own MAI-Base-1 from June - though the comparisons are
against open-weight models (DeepSeek, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8, MiMo-V2.6-Pro) rather
than closed frontier systems. It attributes the gains to data quality and
engineering, including MoE in every layer (MoE-layer MFU up from 24% to 35%),
a dropless MoE design, the Muon optimiser and activation-gradient clipping,
with the corpus up about 36% in unique tokens (vision data 18% of the mix).
Microsoft stresses the model is built on organic data "not distillation from
other models," giving it clean provenance to license weights to trusted
partners via Foundry. MAI-Base-2 is now in post-training, with MAI-Base-3
already in preparation, extending Microsoft's push to build its own models as
it reduces internal reliance on Anthropic and OpenAI.**Nscale - Flagship
Norway data centre runs six months late ahead of a planned $3bn IPO, as
neocloud credit stress mounts**  
Nscale's flagship data centre in Glomfjord, Norway, just north of the Arctic
Circle, is six months behind schedule after cooling-system leaks, local
regulations, construction delays and a fire, with only 6.4MW of a planned 30MW
operational, per Bloomberg. To accelerate the build, a roughly 220-room
floating hotel (the Kalmar, once used to detain migrants) has been towed in to
house hundreds of construction workers, and Nscale has booked most of the
town's hotels, which have sat largely empty since August. Glomfjord is one of
about a dozen planned Nscale sites across Europe and the US, and the setbacks
highlight the risk neoclouds carry in negotiating power, water and land,
securing Nvidia chips amid hardware shortages, and honouring contracts that
can let customers walk away from parts of deals if there are delays. Nscale is
seeking to raise up to $3bn in an IPO as soon as this month, as investor
wariness grows: CoreWeave shares fell 15% on Wednesday and its credit-default-
swap protection hit a record on Thursday, pricing in a more than 60% chance of
default within five years, while an Australian data-centre firm abandoned its
IPO last week. Nscale declined to comment, citing its pre-IPO quiet
period.**RDDT (Sell) - Google updates how AI Search cites**  
Per Google’s blog y’day, AI Mode/Overviews will show inline links higher up in
answers, more prominent related articles and expanded news carousels,
alongside testing top-of-response links to official sites, as Google tries to
do more to feed the open web that generates the content it relies on. In our
view, directionally +ve read-x for Reddit, as Google makes clicking through to
sites easier. However, i) clicks from AI answers have remained minimal after
all previous Google efforts to help site traffic from AI, as users can still
get the answer in the AI Overview without clicking - same again here; and ii)
the changes are mostly focused on professional content (journalism), rather
than user generated content. This could mirror a shift ChatGPT has taken to
prioritise professional content over user-generated content, as the latter has
been shown vulnerable to spam degredation.

## Semis & Hardware

**NVDA (Buy) / TSMC (n/r) - Taiwan plans US AI supply-chain parks, starting in
Texas**  
Taiwan plans multiple US industrial parks costing $2-4bn each, starting with a
Texas complex, to help smaller suppliers to TSMC and AI server assemblers
establish US operations. The manufacturers’ association will raise funding,
with government support including loan guarantees and help securing visas and
land. The parks would span components from packaging substrates to cooling
modules. Separately, TSMC is exploring Texas for further investment but has
not confirmed a location.

## Media

**NFLX (Buy): senior figures responsible for content production exit.
**Variety is reporting that Netflix's Chief Content Officer Bella Bajaria is
departing. This follows yesterday's news that Doug Belgrad, who was in charge
of Originals, and Sheroum Kim, the director of film, have also left. Bajara is
to be replaced by Peter Rice, who was head of content at Disney until 2022.
Investor concerns about the strength of engagement growth have been mostly
responsible for the shares' c50% derating since last year. Puck is speculating
that hiring Rice, who helped Disney manage the merger and integration of 21st
Century Fox, is a signal of the company's interest in further acquisitions,
like for NBCUniversal, which may soon be up for sale. We tend to think that
the market's intense focus on engagement is myopic, but also view acquiring
studios for content as a good use of Netflix's strong balance sheet.

| Broadcom and Intel cite capital as a major constraint Broadcom noted that
"financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of
semiconductors, memory chips or electricity". Intel similarly had concerns
regarding capital and ROI.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fff8))CoreWeave
seeks investment-grade rating to access insurance capital CoreWeave noted that
it is looking for investment-grade offtakes to help attract insurance capital
to its chip-backed debt. The comments come as investor fears around timing
inconsistencies between data center leases and customer contracts increase and
credit default swaps hit all-time highs.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fff9))Apple to
release Apple Intelligence in China in December Following regulatory delays
over the span of two years, Apple Intelligence is expected to launch in China
in December. Apple Intelligence reportedly has guardrails developed with
Alibaba, with updates requiring government approval. Further, Apple is working
with Baidu "on features related to search and Siri". However, Siri AI is not
expected to be a part of the rollout.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fffa))Nvidia and
Cisco announce Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) The module is
designed to support 400 Gb/s lane speeds and 16 full-duplex lanes, allowing
for double the lane counts and double the lane bandwidths of 200 Gb/s per lane
octal small form factor (OSFP) optics. The new modules are also 1.3 times as
power efficient as the previous 200 Gb/s generation.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fffb))Lumentum,
Astera Labs, and Corning show VCSEL PCIe over optics for scale-up Lumentum,
Astera Labs, and Corning have jointly demonstrated PCIe-over-optics, designed
to extend connectivity within a rack. The proof-of-concept product contains
Astera Labs' Scorpio Smart Fabric Switch, Lumentum's 1060 nm VCSEL-based
optical interconnect platform, and Corning's multimode fiber.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fffc))CXMT
announces plans to release new server-memory product by end of 2026 CXMT
announced "key progress" on a new, smaller footprint memory cell. The
company's "4F square" design reduces cell surface area to 4F² or four times
the square of the minimum semiconductor line width versus prior 6F²
architectures.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fffd))Meta
releases newest model, Wonder Meta released its newest AI model, Muse Wonder,
designed to power its AI assistant. Subscriptions of $20 a month and $100 a
month will be offered to Muse users.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6fffe))Microsoft
reveils Maia 300 Microsoft unveiled its newest Maia 300 accelerators, noting
that it will make Maia the primary inferencing system for its products, with
deployments starting in 2027. The firm expects to use 96 Maia 300 chips per
data center rack, allowing for seven times more tokens per rack and 40% more
tokens per MW than merchant GPUs.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf6ffff))Oracle urges
expedited approval of natural gas pipeline for Project Jupiter Oracle has
asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to fast-track authorization of
its pipeline in New Mexico as regulation process timelines threaten to delay
the project. The pipeline is set to move 400M cubic feet of natural gas per
day to power the data center. In light of the project being delayed to
February 2027, Oracle is considering trucking natural gas supplies to the site
to begin commissioning work.
([Source](https://neo.ubs.com/r/7/?id=h7ea74606,d1d790a,4bf70000))Amazon looks
to buy Decart for $7B AI startup Decart's Lucy model is capable of editing
live video, while its Oasis model generates simulated environments for
robotics and autonomous driving tests. Decart was last valued near $4B in May.
